text: Every attack you've studied so far in this course happens after a model is already trained and deployed. Data poisoning is different — it targets the model before it exists, by corrupting the data it learns from. If an attacker can influence a training set, a fine-tuning set, or a feedback loop a deployed model keeps learning from, they can shape what that model believes is normal or correct long before any security team ever sees a running system to defend.

Poisoning isn't one thing — it splits into real risk categories you need to tell apart. Availability attacks flood a training set with noisy or mislabeled data to broadly degrade accuracy, and they're usually the easiest to catch, because the damage shows up in overall evaluation metrics. Targeted, or integrity, attacks are narrower and far more dangerous: the model behaves normally almost everywhere, except for one specific, chosen condition, which means overall accuracy barely moves and standard testing misses it. Feedback-loop poisoning targets systems that keep learning from live user input after deployment — a chatbot, a recommender, a spam filter — through a channel that was never validated.

Microsoft's Tay chatbot is a real, well-documented example. Released on Twitter in 2016, Tay was designed to learn conversational patterns from live user interactions. Within about sixteen hours, coordinated users fed it a stream of offensive input, and Tay began reproducing it — a textbook case of feedback-loop poisoning against a live learning system. Microsoft pulled it offline the same day. The lesson isn't about chatbots specifically; it's that any system learning from unvalidated live input carries this exact risk, whether that's a bot from 2016 or a modern pipeline that logs user corrections back into fine-tuning data.

That's why this course treats training data as a protected asset, with the same kind of scrutiny you'd give any other sensitive system — who can write to it, who can read it, and whether anything unusual gets noticed before it's baked into a model's weights. And because poisoning splits into those three distinct categories, each one needs its own kind of watching: broad statistical checks for availability attacks, much narrower behavioral testing for targeted attacks, and tight validation on any channel a deployed system uses to keep learning.

Next, in Lesson 10, we widen the lens from the training data itself to everything around it — the pretrained models and datasets most teams pull in rather than build from scratch. That turns out to be a supply chain problem you already understand from software, just pointed at model weights and datasets instead of packages.
